records.text: Checklists Practical, repeatable checklists for using decision records — from deciding whether one is warranted, through writing, reviewing, and running the practice across an organization. Contents: Checklist: does this decision need a decision record? Checklist: before you start writing Checklist: while writing Checklist: before you publish for comment Checklist: review and approval Checklist: after the decision (rollout) Checklist: running decision records across an organization Checklist: quarterly or annual decision log audit Checklist: does this decision need a decision record? Write one if you answer yes to any of these: [ ] Would reversing this decision be costly, slow, or embarrassing? [ ] Does it affect people outside the room where it's being decided? [ ] Is it likely someone will ask "why did we do it this way?" a year from now? [ ] Are there genuinely contested options, with reasonable people on different sides? [ ] Does it set a precedent or policy other decisions will need to be consistent with? [ ] Would a new hire or a new leader in this role benefit from knowing the reasoning? Skip a decision record if all of these are true: [ ] It's cheap and fast to reverse. [ ] It affects only the decision-maker or a single self-contained team. [ ] It's already fully covered by existing policy, standard, or documentation. [ ] It's explicitly temporary — a workaround, pilot, or time-boxed experiment. Checklist: before you start writing [ ] Named decision-maker(s) identified — one person, or a specific committee/rule for how the group decides. [ ] Real stakeholders identified — who needs to weigh in before this is final? [ ] Deadline or urgency understood — does this have to be decided now, or can it wait for more information? [ ] Chose lightweight vs. comprehensive template based on stakes (see template/index.md). [ ] Know where the finished record will be stored, so it isn't lost in a chat thread or a single person's inbox. Checklist: while writing [ ] Title is short, present-tense, and active — states the decision, not the topic. [ ] Context explains the situation to a reader with zero meeting background. [ ] At least two genuinely viable options are listed, including "do nothing" if relevant. [ ] Each option's trade-offs are stated as facts, not as a strawman built to make the favored option win. [ ] Decision is written in plain active voice: "We will do X" — not a pros/cons summary standing in for a decision. [ ] Consequences describe what changes next, not a rehash of the options debate. [ ] Related decisions, requirements, or documents are linked, if any exist. [ ] The whole thing focuses on exactly one decision — split it if you find two. Checklist: before you publish for comment [ ] A stranger to the discussion could read it and understand both the decision and why. [ ] No unresolved "did you consider X?" gaps — if a likely question isn't answered, add it. [ ] Status is set correctly (usually request for comments or proposed at this stage). [ ] Comment deadline and process are stated explicitly (e.g., "comments by Friday, then default-accepted"). [ ] The record is one page or close to it — if it's sprawling, check whether it's actually more than one decision. Checklist: review and approval [ ] Every named stakeholder had a real chance to comment, not just a courtesy CC. [ ] Substantive comments are reflected in the record (as edits or as an added, dated note) — not just acknowledged and ignored. [ ] The named decision-maker explicitly accepted, rejected, or sent it back — silence is not acceptance. [ ] Status field is updated to match the outcome ( accepted , rejected , etc.) with a date. [ ] If rejected or deferred, the record still stays in the log rather than being deleted — it documents that the question was raised and why it didn't proceed. Checklist: after the decision (rollout) [ ] Decision is communicated to everyone it affects, not just those who were in the room. [ ] Follow-on requirements, budget, or training implications from the "Consequences" section are actually assigned to someone. [ ] The record is filed in the shared decision log, not left in a personal folder or a chat thread. [ ] An accountable owner is named for future review of this decision. [ ] If this decision supersedes a previous one, the old record's status is updated to superseded with a link forward. Checklist: running decision records across an organization [ ] Decided who can propose a decision record (commonly: anyone). [ ] Decided who can approve one, and whether that varies by decision type, dollar threshold, or risk level. [ ] Decided the escalation path when stakeholders disagree. [ ] Chosen a storage location every relevant team will actually use. [ ] Chosen a naming convention people can adopt without a program manager — "decisions" is often more approachable than "decision records." [ ] Identified a small number of early, high-visibility decisions to record first, to demonstrate value before mandating anything. [ ] Avoided turning this into forced paperwork — introduced it as something that makes a team's own life easier, not a top-down compliance requirement. Checklist: quarterly or annual decision log audit [ ] Skim for records stuck in request for comments or proposed with no resolution — close them out or explicitly archive them. [ ] Check that accepted decisions with a stated review cadence were actually reviewed. [ ] Check for decisions that were informally reversed in practice but never marked superseded in the log — update them. [ ] Spot-check a few older records: would a new hire today understand the context without asking someone? [ ] Confirm the log is still stored somewhere the current team actually uses — tooling and habits drift over a year.

records.title: Examples
records.text: Examples Starting points for teams that are considering a kind of decision, across business functions. Each example uses the comprehensive template and is a work in progress with the status request for comments : it shows how a team makes progress, debates the options, and gathers information. None of them records a finished decision. Read one or two close to your own domain, then replace the fictional context with your own. See the tutorial for a guided walkthrough instead. Enter the mid-market segment: Strategy Select a CRM platform: Sales Reposition the brand around reliability: Marketing Usage-based pricing: Product Hybrid remote-work policy: Human Resources Reduce single-vendor concentration risk: Risk Build vs. buy for a project: Project / Operations Business frameworks: Strategy / Operations Choose the primary database: Technology / Architecture Target operating model: Strategy / Operations Choose a hybrid working model: Human Resources Choose between a product business and a service business: Strategy Weigh public value in a service redesign: Public Sector Weigh health economics in a treatment funding decision: Health Written ways of working: Operations Workplace reasonable adjustments: Human Resources ITIL 5: Technology / Operations The Agile Manifesto: Technology / Operations Six Sigma: Operations / Quality Lean manufacturing: Operations / Manufacturing Extreme Programming: Technology / Software Engineering Project portfolio management: Project / Operations Workplace planning and management: Operations / Facilities Contact relationship management: Sales / Customer Choose our information technology frameworks: Technology / Operations Notes on this index: Each example is one self-contained file — the same convention recommended for your own decision log. Every example has the status request for comments and a Decision section that says "Not yet decided". The examples model how a team frames the issue, tests assumptions, compares options, and decides how it will decide, not what to decide. Details are deliberately generic. Staff counts, currencies, and prices are left out; each example describes how the decision team could estimate costs, benefits, and trade-offs in its own terms. The Related notes section of each example lists sources to learn more: Wikipedia articles, ISO standards, videos, and other references. Every example uses the comprehensive template, so you can see each section at work. For everyday decisions, the lightweight template keeps just the core fields; see template/index.md for how to choose. A technology example is included even though the target audience is business, technology, and strategy leaders together — architecture decisions are one instance of this same general pattern, not a separate discipline.

records.title: The Agile Manifesto
records.text: The Agile Manifesto Status: request for comments Date: 2026-02-16 Decision-maker(s): Chief Technology Officer (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Delivery Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering how to introduce the values and principles of the Agile Manifesto into how delivery teams plan and work. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate the options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue Delivery teams currently work in long, planned projects with fixed scope and hand-offs between analysis, build, and test. Releases are infrequent, and customers often receive something that no longer matches what they need. Leaders are interested in the values and principles of the Agile Manifesto: individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, and responding to change. The team is also aware that "agile transformations" often fail when ceremonies are imposed without the change underneath them. The questions to answer: What problems are we trying to solve, and how would we know they are solved? Do the manifesto's values fit our products, customers, contracts, and regulation, or only some of them? How do we introduce the values so that behaviour changes, not only meeting names? Who goes first, and what happens to teams that do not? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Shorter feedback loops would help our customers. Test: ask customers and delivery teams how often they would want to see working software, and what stops that today. Volunteer teams will adopt the values in substance. Test: look at what volunteers actually want to change, and whether they have sponsors. Our contracts and governance allow more frequent, smaller releases. Test: check contract terms, approvals, and compliance steps for what blocks frequent delivery. Working software delivered frequently is a fair measure of progress. Test: agree on how to observe it (time from idea to customer, release frequency, customer feedback). Constraints Commitments to customers in fixed-scope contracts cannot change automatically; each will need its own conversation. The organization will probably run two ways of working side by side for some time. Teams still have to deliver while they learn. Unknown, to be confirmed: budget for coaching or training, and any regulatory or audit steps that assume a particular lifecycle. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and write down the evidence that would change the team's mind. Mandate one agile method for every team from a fixed start date. Value: consistency and a clear signal from leadership. Cost drivers: training for everyone; role changes; tool changes; time lost while teams adapt; the cost of discovering later that the method suits some teams badly. Timeline shape: fast start; long tail of correcting course. Risks: ceremonies without change; people who are not ready perform them without changing how they work. Adopt by team, starting with volunteers. Teams that want to try it release in short cycles, choose practices that fit them, and show results; the manifesto's values are the guide. Value: real local examples; practices tied to values. Cost drivers: coaching time; running two ways of working; effort to collect and share what is learned. Timeline shape: waves, with later waves joining once earlier teams have run long enough to show results. Capabilities needed: sponsors; a way to measure outcomes; people who can coach. Risks: uneven adoption; volunteers are not typical of the whole organization. Bring in an outside coaching organization to lead the change. Value: experience and speed. Cost drivers: fees; the cost of dependency; the knowledge that leaves when the engagement ends. Risks: capability may not stay in the company. Adopt only selected practices (for example short cycles and regular retrospectives) without adopting the wider values. Cheaper, but may leave the underlying problems unaddressed. Keep the current approach and fix specific delivery problems directly. A real baseline. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Method or mindset? The manifesto is a set of values and principles, not a specific method. Teams choose among methods (such as Scrum, Kanban, or Extreme Programming). How much choice should teams have? Fixed scope versus responding to change. How far do existing contracts and budgets constrain what teams can do? Who is measured on what? If teams are still measured on plan adherence, frequent change will feel risky. Speed of rollout versus depth. What does the team lose by going slower, and what does it risk by going faster? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Cost the options in the organization's own terms: training and coaching time, role changes, tool changes, contract renegotiation, productivity dip during transition. Show ranges rather than single figures. Choose outcome measures before starting: time from idea to working software in customers' hands, release frequency, defects found after release, customer feedback, team satisfaction. Avoid counting ceremonies. Compare options under best, likely, and worst scenarios, and ask which option leaves the organization best placed if it stalls. Use a weighted decision matrix for value, cost, risk, speed, fit with contracts, and capability needed. Run a pre-mortem: assume the change failed and write down why. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and by when. Agree the criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence listed under Assumptions and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team chooses a team-by-team approach, it would need to: Name a sponsor and a person who collects what volunteer teams learn. Say openly which teams go next, in what order, and why, so teams that move later do not feel left behind. Decide how to handle fixed-scope commitments when each contract comes up for renewal. Agree a stopping rule: if early teams show no improvement after a stated period, pause and record what was learned. Treat practices as a choice for each team within the manifesto's values. Related decisions Extreme Programming: specific engineering practices that fit agile values. Choose our information technology frameworks: how agile fits with other frameworks. Business frameworks: the same staged-adoption pattern applied to goal setting. Decisions not yet made: contract changes; coaching; tooling. Related notes Open items: list which teams have volunteered and why; check which contracts and approvals assume a fixed plan; agree outcome measures. Learn more: Wikipedia: Agile software development, Scrum), Kanban (development)), Cynefin framework, Conway's law ISO: ISO 21502:2020, Guidance on project management, ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Software life cycle processes Video: Agile Product Ownership in a Nutshell (Henrik Kniberg) Read: Manifesto for Agile Software Development and its twelve principles; DORA

records.title: Business frameworks
records.text: Business frameworks Status: request for comments Date: 2026-10-01 Decision-maker(s): CEO and executive team (to be confirmed) Owner: Chief of Staff Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering how to introduce a company-wide goal-setting framework such as Objectives and Key Results (OKRs). It shows how a team can frame the question, debate the options, and gather evidence. It does not record a decision. Issue Leadership is considering a common goal-setting framework, because teams currently set goals in different formats and at different rhythms, and leaders cannot easily see how team work connects to company priorities. Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) is the leading candidate, but the team has not yet agreed that OKRs are the right framework at all. A past attempt to roll out a new planning process everywhere at once stalled: managers were not trained, the tooling was unsettled, and people treated it as extra reporting. The questions the team needs to answer: Is a shared framework the right response to the visibility problem, or is something simpler enough? If yes, is OKRs the right framework, or would another approach (for example a balanced scorecard, or management by objectives) fit better? How should the framework be introduced: all at once, in phases, or only at the top? What would make a phase "done", so the next one can start? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test, not something to take for granted. Teams will use the framework if it saves them effort. Test: interview a few teams about how they set and track goals today and what they would give up. A small pilot is representative. Test: choose pilot teams that differ in kind (for example one customer-facing, one product, one support) and check whether their experience diverges. Leaders will make time for training. Test: ask leaders what they would stop doing to make room, and check calendars before committing. The visibility problem is caused by inconsistent goals, not by something else such as unclear priorities or weak reporting. Test: trace two or three company priorities down to team work and see where the link breaks. Constraints A previous rollout stalled, so patience for a repeat is limited. Confirm what exactly went wrong last time. Managers need to be trained before their teams are asked to use the framework. Tooling choice should follow what the pilot teams actually need, but some interim way of recording goals is needed from the start. Unknown, to be confirmed: how the framework relates to existing planning, budgeting, and performance cycles, and what leadership will and will not link to it. Options considered For each option the team should estimate value, cost, timeline, and capability needs, and write down what evidence would change its mind. Introduce everywhere at the same time. Value: one shared language quickly; no period of two systems side by side. Cost drivers: training for every manager at once; time for every team to write and review goals; support load on whoever owns the framework; the cost of a failed rollout (lost credibility). Timeline shape: short to start, long to stabilize. Problems are found by everyone simultaneously. Capabilities needed: trained facilitators at scale; settled tooling. Risks: repeats the conditions of the earlier stall. Introduce in stages: leadership team, then a few pilot departments, then everyone. Value: each phase teaches the team what to change before the next; early examples persuade skeptics. Cost drivers: a longer period of running two goal-setting approaches; extra coordination; extra training and review time for the pilot teams, which should be budgeted explicitly. Timeline shape: sequential phases, each lasting long enough to complete at least one full goal cycle including scoring and review. Capabilities needed: a named owner; written exit criteria for each phase; a way to gather pilot feedback. Risks: momentum fades between phases; pilot teams are not representative. Adopt only at the leadership level. Value: lowest effort and risk. Cost drivers: small, but the benefit may be small too. Risks: does not solve visibility below the leadership team. Do nothing new, and instead fix the visibility problem another way (for example a simple shared priorities document). Worth costing honestly as the baseline against which the other options are judged. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Speed versus learning. Moving everywhere at once is faster but gives no chance to fix the framework before everyone depends on it. How much is the speed worth? Fit versus fashion. OKRs are widely discussed, but the team should ask what problem they solve here and what a good outcome looks like in terms of observable change. Cost of two systems. Phasing means some teams work in the old way for a while. Is that acceptable, and for how long? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: List one-time costs (design, training, facilitation, tooling set-up) and recurring costs (time spent writing, reviewing, and scoring goals; tool licences; owner time) in the organization's own terms, such as person-time and spend, as ranges rather than single numbers. List benefits the team can observe: fewer duplicated or conflicting goals, faster alignment conversations, better ability to trace work to priorities. Compare options under at least three scenarios (works well, works partly, stalls) and ask which option is least regretted if it stalls. Use a simple weighted decision matrix for criteria such as learning, speed, risk, cost, and fit with existing planning. Run a pre-mortem: assume the rollout failed in a year and list the reasons. Decision Not yet decided. This record is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision once the questions above are answered. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides (a person, or a rule such as consensus with escalation after a stated period). Agree the criteria and their weights before comparing options. Gather the evidence listed under Assumptions, and record what was found. Share the record for comment with a deadline, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team does choose a phased approach, it would need to: Name an owner and publish exit criteria for every phase (for example leaders trained, a full cycle scored, pilot teams report the process is worth the time). Budget time for training and review explicitly, rather than absorbing it silently. Decide tooling late, using what the pilot teams needed. Agree what happens if a phase misses its criteria: repeat it, adjust the framework, or stop. Decide separately, and later, whether to link the framework to pay or performance reviews. Related decisions Target operating model: how the framework fits the wider way the organization runs. Choose our information technology frameworks: the same staged-adoption question applied to several frameworks at once. Decisions not yet made: tooling for recording goals; whether to link goals to compensation or performance review. Related notes Open items: confirm what went wrong in the earlier rollout; identify candidate pilot departments; ask managers what they would need to see written down before a first phase starts. Learn more: Wikipedia: Objectives and key results, Management by objectives, Balanced scorecard, Change management, John Kotter ISO: ISO 9001:2015, Quality management systems, ISO 37000:2021, Governance of organizations Video: Why the secret to success is setting the right goals (John Doerr, TED); What is John Kotter's 8-Step Process for Managing Change? (Mike Clayton) Read: What Matters; Measure What Matters (John Doerr); Leading Change (John P. Kotter)

records.title: Contact relationship management
records.text: Contact relationship management Status: request for comments Date: 2026-10-12 Decision-maker(s): Chief Revenue Officer (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Revenue Operations Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering how to manage contacts and relationships with customers, partners, and suppliers in one shared way, including consent. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue Customer and partner contacts are held in individual inboxes, personal spreadsheets, and several different tools. When an account manager leaves, their relationships leave too, and the same person has been contacted on the same day by different teams. The organization also cannot show where a person's consent to be contacted is recorded. The questions to answer: Who needs contact information, for what, and who owns it? What data do we hold, where, and how good is it? What do we need to record about consent and preferences, and how do we answer requests to see, correct, or delete personal data? Which solution fits the whole organization, not only sales? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Account managers will log interactions in a shared system if it is easy and their relationships stay theirs to work. Test: ask them what they would need, and run a trial. Existing data is good enough to migrate after cleaning and merging duplicates. Test: sample records and measure duplicates and gaps. One system can serve several teams (sales, support, partners, suppliers). Test: map each team's needs and see where they differ. Consent can be recorded reliably in the new system. Test: define the consent model with Legal and check what each option supports. Constraints Consent and contact preferences must be recorded in one place, and requests from a person must be answerable from that record. Rules on who may see and change which records must be agreed before migration. Migration takes staff time. Unknown, to be confirmed: the legal requirements that apply (for example the GDPR), data retention rules, and contract terms of current tools. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Keep the current mix of tools and spreadsheets. Value: no cost or change effort. Risks: lost relationships, duplicate contact, and unclear consent continue. Adopt one shared contact relationship management system for the whole company. Value: one record per person and organization; shared history; recorded consent. Cost drivers: licences; data migration; integration; training; administration; the effort of cleaning data. Risks: change in habits; rules for access need design. Add contact management to the existing sales CRM only. Value: quickest; the tool is known. Risks: leaves out partners, suppliers, and non-sales teams. Phased rollout starting with the teams that feel the pain most, retiring other tools once their data has moved. Master data approach. Keep specialist tools but create one trusted record of each contact, shared through integration. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Scope. Customers only, or also partners, suppliers, and others? Ownership of relationships. The company, not the individual, should hold the record. How do we make people comfortable with this? Privacy. Collect only what is needed; record the lawful basis, including consent where it applies. Cost of cleaning data. Often more than expected. How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: List the data held in each place, its quality, and its risks. Estimate costs over a stated horizon in the organization's terms: licences, migration, cleaning, integration, training, administration, and exit. Show ranges. Estimate benefits: fewer lost relationships, less duplicate contact, faster answers to data requests, better reporting. Assess privacy and security: consent handling (ISO/IEC 29184 describes online notices and consent), security controls (ISO/IEC 27001), and privacy management (ISO/IEC 27701). Choose measures: share of contacts with owner and consent recorded, duplicates, time to answer a request, and usage by teams. Review after the first period. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who must be consulted (Legal, Sales, Support, Partnerships). Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides on one shared system, it would need to: Name a lead for selection, migration, and rules for access. Record consent and contact preferences on the record, and handle requests from that record. Check usage in the first period and adjust the process, not only the reminders, if people do not log interactions. Clean and merge duplicate contacts during migration. Retire other tools once data has moved. Related decisions Select a CRM platform: the choice of tool this builds on. Decisions not yet made: data retention; access rules; integration with other systems. Related notes Open items: inventory where contacts are held; sample data quality; ask Legal to review consent fields. Learn more: Wikipedia: Customer relationship management, Contact manager, Master data management, Data quality, General Data Protection Regulation, Consent ISO: ISO/IEC 29184:2020, Online privacy notices and consent, ISO/IEC 27701:2025, Privacy information management systems, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Information security management systems Read: UK ICO: consent; Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR)

records.title: Extreme Programming
records.text: Extreme Programming Status: request for comments Date: 2025-10-06 Decision-maker(s): Head of Engineering (to be confirmed) Owner: Engineering Manager Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for an engineering team that is considering how to introduce practices from Extreme Programming (XP), such as test-driven development, pair programming, continuous integration, and small releases. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate the options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue Product teams ship features in large batches, and defects found late are expensive: a noticeable share of releases need an urgent fix after release. Engineering leaders are interested in practices from Extreme Programming, an agile software development method that emphasizes technical practices such as test-driven development, pair programming, continuous integration, small releases, refactoring, and collective code ownership. These practices support each other, but they also change how engineers work every day. Adopting all of them at once is likely to meet resistance and to be done superficially. The questions to answer: Which problems do we want to solve (late defects, slow feedback, knowledge held by a few people), and which practices address them? In what order should practices be introduced, and who goes first? What would we measure to know that the practices are helping? What is the right balance between a shared standard and each team's choice? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Late defects are mainly caused by lack of fast automated feedback. Test: trace a sample of urgent fixes back to where the defect could have been caught. The foundational practices (continuous integration and automated tests) make the others possible. Test: ask teams that have tried the practices which ones depended on which. Engineers will adopt practices they see working in a team beside them. Test: ask engineers what would persuade them, and what worries them. The rate of urgent fixes after release is a fair measure of progress. Test: agree how it will be counted, and check that other measures (lead time, change failure rate) do not tell a different story. Constraints Teams still have to deliver features while they learn, so output in the first period will probably be lower. Engineers should keep a choice about how they pair and which tools they use. Existing build and test infrastructure may need work before continuous integration is useful. Unknown, to be confirmed: how much of the codebase is testable today, and whether regulatory or customer constraints affect release frequency. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Adopt all practices at once in every team. Value: practices reinforce each other. Cost drivers: training; slower delivery during learning; tooling work across all teams at once. Risks: large change; teams without the underlying skills may abandon the practices within weeks. Adopt the practices in a chosen order, team by team. For example continuous integration and automated tests first (the foundations), then small releases and pair programming, then test-driven development. Value: each practice has time to settle; early ones make later ones possible; the first team's experience guides the rest. Cost drivers: coaching; time for pairing and writing tests built into plans; infrastructure work for the pipeline. Timeline shape: sequential, with the next team joining when the previous team has kept its release pipeline healthy for a stated period. Capabilities needed: a coach; a reliable build pipeline; manager support for the dip in output. Risks: slow; practices adopted unevenly. Adopt only the easy practices. Low effort, but may skip those with the largest benefit, such as automated testing. Adopt a different set of practices (for example those described by DORA research on software delivery, such as continuous delivery, trunk-based development, and loosely coupled architecture) and treat XP as one source among several. Do nothing new and address specific causes of defects directly. A real baseline. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Pair programming. A practice many engineers are wary of. Where does it help (knowledge sharing, complex work), and where does it not? Standardize or let teams choose? Shared outcomes (fewer urgent fixes, faster feedback) with team freedom in how to reach them, or a stricter standard? Quality versus speed in the short term. Are leaders willing to accept lower output while teams learn? TDD, a means or an end? Some practices (such as test-driven development) are debated even among experienced practitioners. The team should decide what problem the practice addresses before adopting it. How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Cost the current approach: effort spent on urgent fixes, delays caused by late defects, customer impact. Use ranges in the organization's own terms. Cost the programme: coaching, training, time for pairing and tests, infrastructure for the pipeline, and the temporary dip in delivery. Choose measures first: share of releases needing urgent fixes, lead time for changes, deployment frequency, time to restore service (the DORA measures), and engineer feedback. Compare options under best, likely, and worst scenarios; ask how the answer changes if the benefit appears later or smaller than hoped. Use a weighted matrix and a pre-mortem. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and by when. Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team chooses a phased approach, it would need to: Name a coach and ask the first team to report honestly on what helped and what did not. Plan time for pairing and for writing tests into delivery plans. Invest in the build and test pipeline before relying on it. Agree a stopping rule: if a practice is not helping after a stated period, the team can propose to stop it and record why. Keep engineers' choice about how they pair and which tools they use; practices should set the outcome, not every detail of how it is reached. Related decisions The Agile Manifesto: the wider decision about values that these practices support. Choose our information technology frameworks: how XP fits with other frameworks. Decisions not yet made: pipeline and tooling investment; code ownership model. Related notes Open items: sample recent urgent fixes; ask engineers about their concerns with pairing and testing; check what the build pipeline can do today. (Agilemania) Read: Extreme Programming: A gentle introduction; Martin Fowler, Continuous Integration; DORA; Extreme Programming Explained (Kent Beck)

records.title: Weigh health economics in a treatment funding decision
headings: Weigh health economics in a treatment funding decision
records.text: Weigh health economics in a treatment funding decision Status: request for comments Date: 2026-05-12 Decision-maker(s): Regional commissioning board (to be confirmed) Owner: Director of Strategic Commissioning Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a health commissioning team that is considering whether and how to fund a new treatment, weighing clinical benefit, cost-effectiveness, budget impact, and equity. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue A new medicine for a long-term condition that affects many people in a region has been proposed for funding. Trial evidence suggests an improvement in quality of life and a reduction in hospital admissions. The budget is fixed, so funding the medicine means funding something else less. A decision based only on price, or only on clinical benefit, ignores that trade-off. The questions to answer: How large and how certain is the benefit, for which patients? What does it cost, and what is the cost per unit of health gained compared with other uses of the same money? What is the budget impact, over several years, and what would be displaced? How does each option affect equity and health inequalities? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Trial results apply to our patients. Test: compare trial populations with local patients, and consider real-world evidence. The group likely to gain most can be identified reliably. Test: define criteria and check against local records. The supplier will agree to terms such as a lower price and data collection. Test: open discussions early. Outcome data can actually be collected with local systems. Test: check what is recorded and what would need new capture. Constraints The budget is fixed. The cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained should be considered against the thresholds and practice used by the decision-making body. Any managed arrangement needs data that can be collected and reviewed. Unknown, to be confirmed: the number of patients, the price and its confidentiality, other treatments, and any national guidance that applies. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Fund for all eligible patients. Value: access for all who are eligible; simple to run. Risks: the budget impact may require cuts elsewhere; cost per QALY may exceed accepted levels. Do not fund. Value: no budget impact; no displacement. Risks: patients lose a treatment with a demonstrated benefit; inequalities may widen for those without other options. Fund for a defined group under a managed-access agreement. For example those who benefit most, with the supplier adjusting the price, collecting outcome data, and a review after a stated period. Value: moves cost per QALY toward accepted levels; limits budget impact. Cost drivers: negotiation; monitoring; data collection; administration. Risks: excludes some patients; depends on supplier agreement and on data that can be collected. Defer while more evidence is gathered, accepting that patients wait. Fund on a time-limited basis with a pre-agreed review. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Efficiency versus equity. A treatment may be cost-effective overall yet benefit groups that are already advantaged more. Evidence and uncertainty. How should the board treat long-term benefit estimated from short trials? Thresholds. Where should the line be and how flexible? The QALY (see the MIDAS explainer) is widely used but also criticized; the team should know its limits. Transparency. What will be published about the reasons? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Use established methods of health technology assessment: cost-effectiveness or cost-utility analysis expressed per QALY gained, with uncertainty shown through sensitivity analysis (see NICE's methods manual for a worked approach). Estimate budget impact over several years under different uptake scenarios, and name what would be displaced. Consider equity: who gains, who is excluded, and the effect on health inequalities. Decide what evidence a managed-access agreement would collect, and what result would change the decision at review. Document the rationale so that it can be explained and challenged. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and under what rules. Agree criteria and weights first, including how equity counts. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment where appropriate, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides on a managed-access arrangement, it would need to: Negotiate the terms; if the supplier will not agree, bring the matter back to the board. Name what is displaced, rather than leaving it unstated. Publish eligibility criteria and the reasons for them. Measure outcomes, including uptake by group, and review equity at the review point. State openly the uncertainty in the evidence. Related decisions Weigh public value in a service redesign: public-sector appraisal with equity in mind. Decisions not yet made: eligibility criteria; review design; data collection. Related notes Open items: assemble the trial evidence; estimate the eligible population; ask the supplier about terms; check data capture. records.title: Hybrid remote-work policy
records.text: Hybrid remote-work policy Status: request for comments Date: 2026-01-08 Decision-maker(s): CEO and Head of People, with executive team input (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of People Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering moving from a fully remote policy to a hybrid policy for people who live within reach of an office. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate the options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue An organization has worked fully remotely for some years. Survey results suggest a split: people who live within commuting distance of an office report less collaboration across teams and slower onboarding for new hires, while people who live far from any office report high satisfaction and cite remote flexibility as a main reason for joining. Leadership must decide whether to keep one policy for everyone, move to a single standard, or keep a split arrangement. The questions to answer: What is the evidence that location affects collaboration, onboarding, and performance here? Which groups would be affected, and how, by each option? How would any in-office expectation be set, explained, and applied fairly? What would we measure, and for how long, to know whether the policy works? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. In-person time improves onboarding and cross-team work. Test: compare onboarding times and collaboration measures for people with different amounts of in-person time, and ask new hires what helped. Treat correlations with care. A policy that applies only to people within commuting distance can be explained as fair. Test: draft the policy and ask a mixed group to say how it feels. Existing offices can host the expected attendance. Test: check capacity, desks, meeting rooms, and the cost of extending. Remote flexibility matters to people who joined for it. Test: look at attrition risk by group, and ask directly. Constraints People hired explicitly as fully remote cannot be required to relocate or attend, under their terms. Any change needs sufficient notice to staff. Rules must be applied consistently within each group of employees to avoid discrimination; take legal advice for your jurisdiction. Unknown, to be confirmed: the costs of space, travel, and any allowances, and requests for adjustments from people with disabilities or caring responsibilities. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Keep fully remote for everyone. Value: keeps current satisfaction; no disruption. Risks: does not address the reported gaps in onboarding and collaboration. Require full-time office attendance for people within commuting distance. Value: directly addresses collaboration and onboarding concerns. Cost drivers: office space and facilities; commuting burden; likely loss of people who joined for flexibility. Hybrid: a number of anchor days each week in the office for people within commuting distance; remote unchanged for others. Value: targets the group where the gap is reported, without changing terms for people hired as remote. Cost drivers: space planning; communication; manager time to apply rules consistently. Team-set rhythms. Teams choose their own days together, within company limits. Pilot first , trying the hybrid model in some locations or teams and comparing results before a wider policy. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Evidence quality. Research on remote and hybrid work exists (for example randomized studies of working from home and surveys of hybrid arrangements), but results depend on the type of work. What applies here? Fairness. Different rules for different groups can feel arbitrary unless the reasons are clear. Autonomy versus coordination. Trust and flexibility versus the benefits of being together. Risk of losing people. Who is most likely to leave, and how costly would that be? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Describe the outcomes wanted (onboarding speed, collaboration, retention, performance, wellbeing) and how each will be measured. Cost each option: space, facilities, travel, management time, communications, and the cost of lost or hard-to-hire people. Show ranges. Consider health and safety and psychological wellbeing, including commuting and isolation. Compare options under best, likely, and worst scenarios. Plan a review after a stated period, with named measures and a rule for what to do depending on what they show. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who is consulted. Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides on a hybrid policy, it would need to: Give staff a full period of notice and say which days apply in each office. Confirm that office capacity supports the expected attendance. Give managers guidance on applying the policy consistently. Track onboarding and collaboration measures for a stated period. Decide how requests for individual adjustments will be handled. Related decisions Choose a hybrid working model: the choices within a hybrid model. Workplace reasonable adjustments: individual needs. Workplace planning and management: how space is planned. Decisions not yet made: whether pay depends on location; future fully remote hiring. Related notes Open items: check onboarding and survey data; ask department heads for evidence; confirm legal advice on applying the policy. records.title: Choose a hybrid working model
records.text: Choose a hybrid working model Status: request for comments Date: 2026-08-20 Decision-maker(s): Executive team (to be confirmed) Owner: Chief People Officer Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is deciding how a hybrid working model should work in practice: how often, which days, how space is used, and how fairness is kept across roles. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue Staff have worked mostly from home for some time without a written policy, and different managers now expect different things. An engagement survey suggests that many staff want to work remotely much of the week, while several managers report that in-person days help onboarding and work across teams. The lease on the main office will end, so the team must also decide how much space to keep. The questions to answer: What do staff, managers, and customers need, and where do they conflict? What in-person time is useful, for which kinds of work? What model is clear, fair across roles, and affordable? How much space do we need, and what flexibility should the lease allow? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Survey responses reflect what staff will actually do. Test: compare stated preferences with badge and booking data, where available. In-person days help onboarding and cross-team work. Test: ask new hires and team leaders what helped; compare teams with different patterns. Teams can agree days that suit their work. Test: pilot with a few teams and see how they decide. A fraction of staff in the office on a typical day is enough capacity. Test: use occupancy data and booking patterns, including peak days. Constraints The lease decision has a deadline. Roles that cannot be done remotely need a fair approach. Some staff will need different arrangements, for example because of a disability or caring duties. Unknown, to be confirmed: costs of space and travel, legal requirements, and local labour market expectations. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Office-first. Everyone is in the office most days. Value: simple; supports in-person learning. Risks: conflicts with what many staff say they want; narrows the hiring pool. Remote-first. No required office days, with space for meetings. Value: lowest property cost; widest hiring pool. Risks: harder onboarding and cross-team work; roles that cannot be done remotely are left in a separate category. Team-set anchor days. Each team chooses a few shared in-person days a week within company limits. Value: fits different kinds of work; keeps benefits of being together. Cost drivers: space planning; booking systems; manager time to apply rules consistently. Company-set days for everyone. Simple and easy to plan space for, but less flexible. Pilot, then decide. Try two models in different parts of the business and compare. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Simplicity versus fit. One rule is easy to explain; different rules fit different work. Evidence. Research suggests hybrid arrangements are often a workable middle (for example work by Nicholas Bloom and colleagues), but results depend on the type of work and on management practice. Fairness. How do we treat roles that cannot be done remotely? Space. Fewer desks reduce cost but require booking and discipline. How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Choose outcome measures: onboarding speed, collaboration, retention, performance, wellbeing, and cost. Estimate costs for each option: space (ranging from several scenarios of attendance), facilities, travel, equipment, management time, and the cost of recruiting if people leave. Show ranges. Consider the effect on health and psychological wellbeing, including isolation and commuting. Compare options under best, likely, and worst scenarios. Plan regular reviews of the measures, with named owners and rules for adjusting. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who is consulted. Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides on team-set anchor days, it would need to: Publish the policy and a template for each team's written agreement. Decide how to handle roles that cannot be done remotely. Introduce desk and room booking. Hold managers accountable for agreeing days and applying rules equally. Review the pattern of each team after a stated period. Related decisions Hybrid remote-work policy: the policy question at company level. Workplace reasonable adjustments: individual needs. Workplace planning and management: how space is planned. Decisions not yet made: pay and location; lease terms. Related notes Open items: collect occupancy and booking data; ask managers what they have seen; check legal requirements. records.title: Choose our information technology frameworks
records.text: Choose our information technology frameworks Status: request for comments Date: 2026-10-14 Decision-maker(s): Chief Information Officer and Chief Technology Officer (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Technology Operations Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a technology group that has been asked to adopt several frameworks (for example ITIL, the Agile Manifesto, Extreme Programming, and Six Sigma) and needs to decide which to use, for which work, and in what order. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue Different leaders have asked the technology group to adopt ITIL for service management, the Agile Manifesto for delivery, Extreme Programming for engineering, and Six Sigma for quality, sometimes in the same teams and the same period. Each request is reasonable alone, but together they overlap, use different vocabularies, and ask people to change faster than they can absorb. The questions to answer: What problem does each framework solve, and for which kind of work? Where do they overlap or conflict, and which should take precedence? In what order should we introduce them, and how many changes can a team absorb at once? How will we know whether the combination helps? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Each framework works best on the kind of work it was designed for. Test: read the sources and talk to people who have used each framework. Teams can absorb one new framework at a time , not several. Test: ask teams what changes are already under way and what capacity they have. Sponsors will accept waiting if they know the order and the reason. Test: talk to them early. A written boundary between frameworks will reduce conflict. Test: draft one and test it on real examples of conflict. Constraints The group has limited capacity for change in any one period. The frameworks use different vocabularies, so shared terms such as incident, change, release, and defect must be defined once. Full adoption of several frameworks could take years. Unknown, to be confirmed: current practice, contractual or audit expectations, and any frameworks already in use. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Adopt every requested framework everywhere. Value: each sponsor gets what they asked for. Risks: overload; conflicting guidance (for example fixed change approvals against continuous release); impossible to tell which change caused which result. Adopt one framework as the single standard. Value: simple to explain. Risks: no one framework covers service operations, product delivery, engineering practice, and quality equally well. Assign each framework to the kind of work it fits, and phase them in one at a time. For example ITIL practices for running live services, the Agile Manifesto's values for how delivery teams plan and work, Extreme Programming practices for building software, and Six Sigma for processes where defects can be measured. Value: clearer for teams; easier to learn from. Cost drivers: a written boundary document; coordination; a long programme. Adopt a governance or standards umbrella such as ISO/IEC 38500 (governance of IT) or ISO/IEC 20000-1, and let teams choose methods within it. Adopt none of them wholesale ; select practices that address the group's measured problems. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Frameworks or outcomes? The aim is better results for customers, not adopting frameworks. Which outcomes matter most? Conflicts. Where guidance conflicts, who decides? Order. Which should go first: the one with the most sponsor pressure, or the one that supports the others? Vocabulary. Shared words reduce friction, but false equivalence hides real differences. How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: List problems and desired outcomes first, with measures (for example from DORA research on software delivery performance, plus service and quality measures). For each framework, estimate costs in the organization's own terms: training, process change, tooling, time lost, and ongoing support. Show ranges. Estimate the capacity for change of each team, and sequence so that no team carries more than it can absorb. Compare options under best, likely, and worst scenarios; choose the one that is easiest to adjust if the evidence changes. Review after the first two frameworks and revisit the order if evidence suggests a better one. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who must be consulted (including the sponsors). Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides to assign frameworks by kind of work and phase them in, it would need to: Name an owner for the boundary document and a way to resolve conflicts, with escalation. Start only one framework in a team at a time, and begin the next only when the previous has met its own exit measures. Tell sponsors of later frameworks the order and the reason now. Define shared terms once, in the boundary document. Review the whole approach after the first two frameworks. Related decisions The Agile Manifesto, ITIL 5, Extreme Programming, and Six Sigma: the decisions on each framework. Business frameworks: the general staged-adoption pattern. Decisions not yet made: tooling; the order of later frameworks. Related notes Open items: list current practices; ask sponsors what outcomes they want; draft a first boundary document. records.title: ITIL 5
records.text: ITIL 5 Status: request for comments Date: 2026-09-30 Decision-maker(s): Chief Information Officer (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of IT Service Management Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for an IT organization that is considering how, and in what order, to adopt ITIL 5 for IT service management. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision, and it does not restate what ITIL 5 says. Issue The IT service desk and the teams around it have grown without a common way of working: incidents, requests, and changes are handled differently by different teams, and recurring incidents are seldom analyzed. Leadership is interested in basing IT service management on ITIL, the widely used guidance for IT service management, in its latest version (ITIL 5), so that internal teams, suppliers, and auditors share practices and vocabulary. ITIL 5 is new and is being released in stages, so the team must first establish what is actually available and stable. The questions to answer: What problem are we trying to solve, and is ITIL 5 the right way to solve it, or is the organization better served by adopting selected practices, staying with the version it already knows, or aligning to the international standard ISO/IEC 20000-1? If the team proceeds, in what order, and at what pace? What do we need to be able to do (capabilities, tools, data) before each step? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. The pain is mainly in a few practices (for example incident, request, and change handling). Test: look at a sample of recent incidents and changes and map where time and quality are lost. Practices can be adopted separately rather than only as a package. Test: read the framework's guidance and talk to organizations that adopted it in stages. The service desk can retrain while running the service. Test: estimate the time each practice needs from staff, against the time they have. Suppliers and auditors will value a common vocabulary. Test: ask the main ones what they currently use and expect. Whether ITIL 5 material is mature enough to adopt now. Test: check what has been published and certified so far, and what is still to come. Constraints The service must keep running during any change; the service desk cannot stop to retrain. Tooling changes should be limited to what a step requires; a large platform change is a separate decision. Old and new ways of working will coexist for a time. The team should say how long that is acceptable. Unknown, to be confirmed: licensing and training cost models for the framework, supplier contract terms that reference a given framework, and any audit or regulatory expectations. Options considered For every option the team should estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note the evidence that would change its mind. Adopt everything at once across all teams. Value: one common way of working soonest. Cost drivers: training for all staff; process redesign for all practices; tooling changes; lost capacity while teams retrain; the cost of reversing a poor start. Timeline shape: short plan, long recovery if it goes poorly. Capabilities needed: strong change leadership and enough spare capacity to absorb the change. Adopt by practice , starting where the pain is greatest and users are most affected (commonly incident and request handling), then change, then problem analysis and continual improvement, with each phase having its own measures. Value: each phase teaches the team what to change in the next; early wins are visible to users. Cost drivers: a longer overall programme; running old and new practices side by side; repeated training; maintaining the exit measures. Timeline shape: a sequence of phases, each long enough to see a measurable change before the next starts. Capabilities needed: reliable service data (resolution time, first-time fix, share of changes causing incidents) and an owner for each practice. Adopt by team : one team adopts all practices first as a pilot, then others follow. Value: a complete working example early. Cost drivers: one service is split across two ways of working while the pilot runs; hand-offs between the pilot team and others become harder. Risks: confuses users and suppliers; the pilot team's context may not be typical. Align to ISO/IEC 20000-1 instead of, or alongside, ITIL. A certifiable requirements standard for a service management system, which some organizations prefer for audit and supplier assurance. Value: external recognition; clear requirements. Cost drivers: assessment and certification effort; documentation. Risks: can encourage a compliance mindset over improvement. Make no framework change yet and fix the specific pains directly. A real baseline option to cost honestly. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Framework or problem? Is the goal to adopt a framework, or to reduce repeat incidents and slow changes? Choose the option that is judged by the second. Pace versus capacity. A faster programme gets benefits sooner but takes the same people away from running the service. Version risk. Adopting something newly released brings fewer worked examples and less training material; staying with a known version is safer but may age. Vocabulary versus practice. Using the same words as suppliers is easier than changing how work is done. Which matters more? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Build a cost model in the organization's own terms. One-time: training, process design, tooling change, consulting, backfill. Recurring: licences, process owner time, audits. Hidden: reduced throughput during transition, supplier contract changes. Give ranges, not single numbers. Choose benefit measures before starting, so success is not defined afterwards: resolution time, first-time resolution, share of changes causing incidents, repeat-incident rate, user satisfaction, audit findings. Estimate payback under best, likely, and worst scenarios, and test how sensitive the answer is to the assumptions the team is least sure of. Score options with a weighted matrix (value, cost, speed, risk, fit with suppliers, capability needed). Ask what each option does to reversibility: which can be stopped after one phase without wasting the work? Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and by when. Settle the criteria and their weights first. Gather the evidence listed above, including what is currently available for ITIL 5. Publish the draft for comment with a deadline, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team chooses a phased approach, it would need to: Publish exit measures for each phase and report against them regularly to the sponsor. Train staff on each practice just before its phase. Keep practices that are not yet in scope running as they do today, and say so. Delay any large service-management platform purchase until the evidence from the first phases is in. Decide what happens when a phase misses its measures: repeat, adjust, or stop. Related decisions Business frameworks: the same staged-adoption pattern applied to a different framework. Choose our information technology frameworks: how ITIL fits with other frameworks the group is considering. Decisions not yet made: tooling; supplier contract changes; certification or not. Related notes Open items: confirm what exists today for ITIL 5; list the practices currently performed well and badly; ask the main suppliers and auditors what they expect. records.title: Lean manufacturing
records.text: Lean manufacturing Status: request for comments Date: 2025-11-24 Decision-maker(s): Plant Director (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Operational Excellence Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering how to introduce lean manufacturing, which focuses on removing waste and delivering what the customer values, in a plant that has several production lines. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue A plant that makes custom products on several production lines has lead times longer than customers expect, work-in-progress stock that fills much of the floor, and operators who report a lot of waiting, rework, and movement of materials. Leaders are interested in lean manufacturing, but a change across the whole plant at once could disrupt orders that must be delivered this year. The questions to answer: Where does time actually go between an order arriving and delivery, and how much of it adds value for the customer? Is lean the right response, and which parts (flow, pull, standard work, problem solving) would help most? Where do we start, how do we involve operators, and when do we extend? What would show that it is working? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Waiting, rework, and movement are the main causes of long lead times. Test: walk the process (go to the "gemba", the place where work happens) and map the flow of one order from start to finish. One line is representative of the others. Test: compare lines on product mix, repeat work, equipment, and staffing. Operators will propose and test improvements if given time and a role. Test: ask operators what they would change and what stops them today. Lead time is a fair measure of progress. Test: agree how lead time, work-in-progress, rework, and on-time delivery will be measured before changing anything. Constraints Orders already promised must be delivered; any change must protect them. Planning must cope with some lines working one way and some another. Operators need protected time for improvement work. Unknown, to be confirmed: equipment constraints, maintenance windows, supplier lead times, and the effect of customer demand swings. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and write down the evidence that would change the team's mind. Change every line at once. Value: fastest route to a consistent plant. Cost drivers: training; changeover; temporary loss of output; management attention across all lines. Risks: threatens delivery of current orders; operators have no time to learn and adjust. Adopt line by line, starting with a pilot line. Map the value stream for one line, reduce waste there, and use the results to choose practices for the rest. Value: contains disruption; operators see real results before their own line changes; learning carries forward. Cost drivers: coaching; operator time for improvement work; running lines in different ways for a time. Timeline shape: sequential, with each line starting only after the previous one has held its improvement for a stated period. Capabilities needed: someone who can lead value-stream mapping; reliable measures; sponsor support. Risks: slow; the pilot line may not be typical. Introduce lean tools plant-wide without redesigning the lines (for example 5S: sort, set in order, shine, standardize, sustain). Value: visible and inexpensive. Risks: improves tidiness without changing flow, so lead times may change little. Combine lean with other methods such as Six Sigma where variation is also a problem. Keep the current approach and fix specific bottlenecks. A real baseline to cost honestly. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Contain risk or move fast? A pilot is safer but slower. How much is speed worth against the risk to current orders? Tools versus system. Lean is a way of thinking about value and flow, not a collection of tools. How much culture change is the team prepared to lead? Which line first? The one with the most repeat work (clearest results), the one with the worst problems (most to gain), or the one with the most willing team (most likely to succeed)? What do operators get? If improvement only means more output, expect little engagement. How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Map the current state and estimate where lead time goes; cost waiting, rework, and inventory in the organization's own terms. Estimate programme costs: coaching, operator time, training, any equipment or layout changes, and the cost of lost output during change. Give ranges. Choose measures first: lead time, work-in-progress, rework, on-time delivery, and some measure of operator engagement or safety. A reference for definitions of manufacturing indicators is ISO 22400-2. Compare options under best, likely, and worst cases, and test how sensitive the answer is to the assumptions the team is least sure about. Use a weighted decision matrix and a pre-mortem. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and by when. Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team chooses a line-by-line approach, it would need to: Name a leader for the pilot, publish the value-stream map and results, and set a lead-time target for the pilot line. Fund operators' time for proposing and testing improvements. Agree what "held" means before starting the next line. Plan around lines that work in different ways during the rollout. Say openly which line is next and under what conditions. Related decisions Six Sigma: a data-driven approach that can complement lean. Choose our information technology frameworks: the general problem of choosing and ordering frameworks. Decisions not yet made: equipment or layout changes; incentives; supplier changes. Related notes Open items: map the current flow of a typical order; compare lines; talk to operators on each line. records.title: Reposition the brand around reliability
records.text: Reposition the brand around reliability Status: request for comments Date: 2026-01-15 Decision-maker(s): CMO (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Brand Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering whether to change the core message of its brand, for example from "innovative" to "reliable". It shows how a team can frame the question, debate the options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue Interviews with customers who won and lost deals suggest that customers often choose the company over faster-moving competitors because of its track record and support, and not because they see it as the most innovative, which is the current brand message. If that is true, the messaging may be working against the reasons customers buy. The team must decide whether to change it, how far, and how. The questions to answer: What do customers and prospects actually value, and how strong is the evidence? How is the brand perceived today, and by whom? If we change the message, what changes with it (visuals, sales material, product claims), and what must stay the same? How would we know that the change helped? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. The reliability advantage is durable , not a temporary effect of a competitor's recent problem. Test: look at the trend over a longer period and in several segments. Existing messaging is not so entrenched that a change would confuse customers. Test: ask customers and the sales team how they describe the company now. Sales and Customer Success can express the new message consistently. Test: run a small pilot with a group of them and compare. Win and loss interviews are representative. Test: check sample size, who was interviewed, and who is missing. Constraints No budget for a full visual rebrand; any change must work within the existing visual system. Claims already made in signed contracts must not be contradicted. Any reliability claim (such as availability statistics) must be independently verifiable before publication. Unknown, to be confirmed: how competitors are positioned, and how much the message appears in product, support, and recruiting. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Keep "innovative" and add proof points. Value: no repositioning risk. Risks: may optimize a message customers do not buy for. Reposition fully around reliability, in phases (for example sales material and paid channels first, wider refresh later). Value: aligns the message with reasons for purchase; phasing limits risk and lets the team learn. Cost drivers: creative work; legal verification of claims; training; updates across channels. Run both messages in parallel by channel. Value: avoids full commitment. Risks: mixed messages may weaken recall; test with data before relying on it. Position around a combination (reliability with a secondary differentiator) so the brand does not read as dull next to a competitor who stresses speed. Do not change the message yet and invest first in better research on customer value. A useful way to structure the debate is the positioning approach described by April Dunford: competitive alternatives, unique attributes, the value they enable, the customers who care most, and the market category that makes the value obvious. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Evidence versus instinct. How much weight do interviews deserve against sales and leadership instincts? Reliable or dull? Sales may worry that "reliable" sounds unexciting against a competitor. Can it be paired with something that gives energy? Depth of change. Message only, or product, support, and hiring too? A message that the company cannot back up damages trust. Speed. Faster change gets benefits sooner; slower change allows learning. How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Define the outcomes expected: win rate in target segments, consideration, sales cycle, brand perception, retention, and referral. Cost the options: research, creative, channel updates, legal review, training, and the cost of mixed messages during transition. Show ranges. Test before committing: message tests with customers, small campaign tests, and a pilot with part of the sales team. Weigh options on value, cost, risk, reversibility, and fit with existing contracts. Run a pre-mortem and name the leading indicators that would trigger a pause. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who must agree (Sales, Legal, Product). Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides to reposition in phases, it would need to: Update sales material and paid channel creative first, and agree how to measure results. Have Legal validate every claim before release. Give Sales and Customer Success talking points and training. Plan a follow-on decision on any wider visual refresh once early results are in. Confirm existing signed contracts are unaffected, since the change would be forward-looking. Related decisions Usage-based pricing: price and positioning affect each other. Decisions not yet made: wider visual refresh; changes to product naming. Related notes Open items: review the quality of win and loss interviews; list claims that would need independent verification; test creative that pairs reliability with a secondary differentiator.
