records.title: Choose between a product business and a service business
headings: Choose between a product business and a service business
records.text: Choose between a product business and a service business Status: request for comments Date: 2026-07-08 Decision-maker(s): CEO and board (to be confirmed) Owner: Chief Strategy Officer Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is deciding whether the company should become mainly a product business, stay mainly a services business, or run both. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue A company earns most of its revenue from custom implementation projects built on a software platform it owns. Projects are profitable but unpredictable, each needs senior engineers, and growth is limited by hiring. Partners increasingly use the platform without the company's services, and investors ask whether it is a product company or a services company. The answer changes whom to hire, how to price, how to measure success, and what to tell customers. The questions to answer: Where does the company actually create and capture value today, by customer and by offer? What do customers value in the custom work, and what would they accept instead? What would each model do to revenue, margin, growth, and risk over time, including during transition? Can partners deliver what customers need? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Customers would accept a more standard offer. Test: interview a sample of customers across segments; separate those who need custom work from those who do not. Partners can deliver to a standard customers accept. Test: pilot with a few partners and measure outcomes. Subscription revenue can replace project revenue. Test: model scenarios using actual customer data, including how long the transition would take. Investors and the board will accept a dip in revenue during transition. Test: ask them directly, and show the scenarios. Constraints Strategic customers value the custom work and must not be abandoned. Revenue may dip during any transition. People in implementation roles would be affected; a separate decision is needed on how to support them. Unknown, to be confirmed: contract terms, partner capacity, and platform readiness for standard onboarding. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Become a product business. Sell the platform by subscription with standard onboarding, and refer custom work to partners. Value: recurring revenue; growth less tied to hiring. Cost drivers: product investment; partner programme; transition support; revenue dip. Timeline shape: a multi-year transition in stages by customer segment. Capabilities needed: product management; pricing; partner management; customer success. Stay a service business. Keep selling implementation projects, and treat the platform as a delivery tool. Value: keeps current revenue and relationships. Risks: growth stays limited by hiring; partners may deliver on the platform at lower cost. Run both with separate economics. Services and product are distinct lines with their own targets, roadmaps, and measures. Value: keeps current revenue while building product revenue. Risks: splits attention; both lines may be under-invested; internal conflict over priorities. Productize selectively. Package the most repeated custom work as standard offers, keeping custom work for large accounts. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Identity. What do we want to be known for, and what do our best people want to do? Transition risk. How long and deep is the revenue dip, and can we fund it? Customer relationships. Moving implementation to partners may weaken the direct relationship. Measures. Product businesses are judged on recurring revenue, retention, and margin; services businesses on utilization and margin per project. Which will we hold ourselves to? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Segment current revenue and margin by customer and offer. Build scenarios (best, likely, worst) for each model over a multi-year horizon, with transition costs, using ranges and stating assumptions. Compare options on revenue quality, margin, growth potential, risk, capability needed, and effect on people and customers. Identify early signals that would show whether the assumptions hold, such as partner delivery results and customer response to standard offers. Run a pre-mortem and agree review points tied to named measures. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides, and what the board needs. Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides to become a product business, it would need to: Publish a multi-year plan, including the order in which customer segments move. Explain the expected revenue dip, and secure agreement to it. Plan support for people whose roles change. Change headline measures to recurring revenue, margin, and retention. Review annually against those measures. Related decisions Target operating model: the organization will need to match. Usage-based pricing: pricing under a product model. Decisions not yet made: partner programme; support for affected staff. Related notes Open items: list customers by dependence on custom work; test partner delivery; model transition scenarios. records.title: Usage-based pricing
records.text: Usage-based pricing Status: request for comments Date: 2026-04-05 Decision-maker(s): VP Product, with CFO input (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Pricing & Packaging Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering whether to change from flat per-seat pricing to a model that charges for usage, or a mix of the two. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate the options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue A software product is priced per seat. The team suspects that this charges light users more than the value they receive, and so contributes to their leaving, while under-charging customers who use the product heavily. Competitors have been moving to usage-based or hybrid pricing, and prospects are asking why the company has not. The questions to answer: What is the product's value metric: what unit of usage tracks the value a customer gets? Do light and heavy customers really behave and feel the way we think? Which pricing model best matches value while keeping revenue predictable enough to plan? How would existing customers move to a new model fairly? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Usage is a good proxy for value. Test: compare usage with customer outcomes and satisfaction across a range of accounts. Light users leave because price feels too high. Test: review cancellation reasons and talk to departed light users. Heavy users will pay more for more value. Test: ask a sample about willingness to pay, and check how sensitive they are to price changes. We can meter and bill usage accurately and transparently. Test: check data quality, and ask customers whether they can predict their bill. Constraints No existing customer should face a net price increase without advance notice. Sales compensation plans must reflect the new structure before it is used for new deals. Finance needs forecasting models that can cope with revenue that varies with usage. Unknown, to be confirmed: contract terms that fix prices, what the billing system can do, and competitor pricing details. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Keep flat per-seat pricing. Value: simple; no migration. Risks: leaves the churn and under-charging issues; competitors differ. Move fully to usage-based pricing. Value: price closely follows value; low barrier to start. Cost drivers: metering, billing and reporting systems; support for bill questions; sales changes. Risks: revenue volatility; customers who dislike unpredictable bills. Hybrid: a base fee plus usage-based charges. Value: more predictable revenue than pure usage pricing, while still addressing light and heavy users. Cost drivers: as above, plus design complexity. Timeline shape: new customers first; existing customers moved after a protected period. Tiered plans with usage limits. A simpler middle path that may meet most of the need. Experiment first , offering the new model to a subset of new customers or a segment, and compare. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Predictability versus fairness. Customers and finance value predictable bills; usage pricing feels fairer but varies. Which metric? Seats, calls, records, outcomes? A poor metric creates the wrong behaviour. Migration. Grandfathering protects customers but delays benefits and complicates operations. Competition. Following competitors is not a reason in itself. What does our evidence say? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Model revenue under each option using existing customer data: for each account, what would it pay under the new model? Show the winners and losers, and the spread, as ranges. Estimate price elasticity qualitatively and through tests, and consider customer reaction to bill changes. Cost the change: metering, billing, support, sales training, legal and contract changes, forecasting tools. Compare the options for revenue level, revenue stability, customer fairness, growth effects, and complexity; test sensitivity to assumptions. Plan an experiment and define in advance what results would lead to scaling it, adjusting it, or stopping. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who must sign off (for example Finance). Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides to move to a hybrid model, it would need to: Model every existing account to confirm no one faces a surprise increase. Update sales compensation and train sales and support. Revise revenue forecasting to handle variation. Contact at-risk light-usage customers early, since they should see their bill fall. Decide separately the exact overage tiers and thresholds. Related decisions Enter the mid-market segment: pricing for a new segment. Reposition the brand around reliability: price signals and positioning. Decisions not yet made: exact usage tiers; migration timeline for existing customers. Related notes Open items: define the value metric candidates; review cancellation reasons; check what billing can meter. Your own billing, usage, and cancellation data is more relevant evidence than any general article. records.title: Build vs. buy for a project
headings: Build vs. buy for a project
records.text: Build vs. buy for a project Status: request for comments Date: 2026-06-01 Decision-maker(s): COO (to be confirmed) Owner: Director of Operations Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that needs a new capability, here a customer-facing scheduling tool, and is deciding whether to build it, buy it, or do something in between. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate the options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue A services business schedules work with a manual, spreadsheet-based process that has caused double-bookings and damaged customer relationships. A fix is needed within a limited time, and the team must decide whether to build a tool internally or buy an existing one. The questions to answer: What must the tool do (requirements), and which of those are essential? How well does each route meet the requirements, within the time available? What is the full cost of each route over its useful life, including what the team gives up by choosing it? What happens if requirements change, or if the chosen route fails? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Most scheduling needs are common to other organizations, so an existing product can cover them. Test: list the requirements and ask vendors to show how each is met. The unusual cases are small enough to handle by workaround. Test: count how often they occur, and write down the workaround for each. Internal engineers can build and maintain the tool. Test: estimate the effort with the people who would do it, and ask what else they would not do. Vendors' timelines are realistic. Test: speak to reference customers of similar size, including those whose projects ran late. Constraints A fix is needed within a fixed period. Other committed product initiatives must keep their timelines, so engineering capacity cannot simply be taken from them. The tool handles customer data, so security and privacy must be checked. Unknown, to be confirmed: integration needs, expected growth, and what happens at the end of a vendor contract. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Build in-house. Value: exact fit to the organization's rules; full control of the roadmap. Cost drivers: design, development, testing, hosting, support and maintenance for the whole life of the tool; the opportunity cost of what engineers do not build instead. Timeline shape: often longer than first estimates; value arrives at the end. Capabilities needed: product management; engineering; operations. Buy an existing product. Value: faster; costs spread; benefits from vendor improvements. Cost drivers: licences, implementation, configuration, training, integration, administration, and exit. Risks: gaps against requirements; vendor changes; lock-in. Buy a product and commission custom work from the vendor. Closes gaps, but adds time and cost, and carries delivery risk. Assemble from smaller tools (for example a low-code platform or a combination of existing services). Improve the manual process first with a stopgap, to buy time for a better decision. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Fit versus speed. A perfect fit that arrives late may be worse than a good fit now. Core or context? Is scheduling part of what makes the business distinctive? If not, buying is usually favoured. Hidden costs. Building has ongoing maintenance; buying has ongoing licences, integration, and exit. Reversibility. Which choice is easier to undo if it proves wrong? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Write requirements and rank them. Score each route against them and note gaps. Estimate total cost of ownership over a stated horizon in the organization's own terms: one-time costs, recurring costs, internal staff time, integration, training, and exit. Show ranges. Estimate the cost of delay: the effect of each additional period of double-bookings. Compare options under best, likely, and worst scenarios, and test the effect of requirement changes. Use a weighted matrix (fit, speed, cost, risk, control, reversibility) and a pre-mortem. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who must agree. Agree requirements and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides to buy, it would need to: Name an implementation lead and plan training within the vendor's timeline. Document workarounds for unsupported cases, log how often they are used, and review after live use. Define what would trigger a follow-on decision on custom work. Confirm that no engineering capacity is taken from committed initiatives. Related decisions Select a CRM platform: a similar choice for a different system. Choose the primary database: a technology instance of build/buy and lock-in questions. Reduce single-vendor concentration risk: dependence on a vendor. Decisions not yet made: custom integration; data retention. Related notes Open items: write and rank requirements; ask vendors for reference customers; estimate build effort with engineers. records.title: Project portfolio management
records.text: Project portfolio management Status: request for comments Date: 2026-10-05 Decision-maker(s): Executive team (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of the Project Management Office Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering how to decide, across the whole organization, which projects to start, continue, or stop. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue An organization runs many active projects across several departments, and each department approves, staffs, and reports on its own. Leaders cannot see the total demand on shared people, such as data engineers who are named on projects whose combined requests exceed their capacity. Projects stall waiting for the same few people, and low-value projects survive because no one compares them with the alternatives. The questions to answer: What are all the projects, what do they cost, and what do they need from shared people? What criteria should decide which projects to start, continue, or stop? Who decides, how often, and with what authority? How much central process is helpful, and how much becomes a bottleneck? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Capacity conflicts are the main reason projects stall. Test: map named people to projects and compare demand with capacity. Departments will supply reliable data. Test: ask for a sample and check how consistent it is. The executive team will stop projects when the evidence says so. Test: look at past decisions to stop projects; ask the team about its appetite. Larger projects account for most of the demand on shared people. Test: sort projects by size and requests. Constraints Smaller projects should stay under departmental control, so the central process does not become a bottleneck. The scoring criteria must be agreed and published in good time. Departments will feel a loss of independence; the benefits must be clear to them. Unknown, to be confirmed: a sensible size threshold, existing project data, and tooling. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Keep departmental decisions. Value: no new process; local autonomy. Risks: capacity conflicts and lack of comparison remain. A central portfolio office approves every project. Value: one view and consistent criteria. Risks: a bottleneck; resistance from departments. Portfolio management with a light central process. A shared list of projects above a set size, common scoring criteria (strategic fit, value, cost, risk, and capacity needed), and a regular executive review to start, continue, or stop projects. Value: one view; deliberate trade-offs without routing small work through a central team. Cost drivers: data collection; the office's time; executive time for reviews. Capabilities needed: reliable data; a decision-making meeting that actually decides. Capacity-first approach. Manage the scarce shared resources (such as the data engineers) first, and extend portfolio rules only if needed. This draws on ideas from the theory of constraints. Adopt a portfolio tool first and let the process follow. Risky if the process is unclear. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Control versus agility. How much central oversight is worth the delay? What counts as value? Financial return, strategic fit, risk reduction, regulatory necessity, and benefits that are hard to quantify. Stopping projects. People find it hard to stop projects already begun; sunk cost is not a reason to continue. Fairness. How does the scoring avoid favouring the loudest department? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Build a first portfolio list and estimate demand by role against capacity, to see how severe the conflict is. Estimate the cost of the current approach in delays, rework, and low-value work. Estimate the cost of the process: the office, data effort, review time, and tools. Test the scoring criteria on past projects: would they have chosen differently, and was that better? Choose measures: share of projects delivered on time, projects stopped early, utilization of shared teams, and benefits realized. Review after a few cycles. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who is consulted. Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides on a light central process, it would need to: Name an owner of the portfolio list and a schedule of reviews. Publish scoring criteria and the size threshold. Ask departments to register projects and capacity by role. Commit the executive team to decide at reviews, including stopping projects, and to record reasons. Review the process after a few cycles. Related decisions Target operating model: how the portfolio fits shared services and customer-aligned teams. Business frameworks: goal setting that portfolio choices can link to. Decisions not yet made: tooling; the benefits tracking approach. Related notes Open items: compile an initial project list; map people to projects; draft scoring criteria. records.title: Weigh public value in a service redesign
headings: Weigh public value in a service redesign
records.text: Weigh public value in a service redesign Status: request for comments Date: 2026-06-18 Decision-maker(s): Director General, with the departmental board (to be confirmed) Owner: Director of Service Design Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a public body that is redesigning a service and wants to weigh public value, not only efficiency. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue A public agency processes a large number of benefit claims. Claims take a long time, and a recent review found that the people who wait longest are those least able to complete the online form: older people, people with limited language skills, and people without reliable internet access. A proposal would move all claims to a digital-only service and close some local offices to save operating cost. Because this is a public service, an efficient choice is not enough. It must also be legitimate, fair, and something the agency can sustain. Mark Moore's public value strategic triangle names these three parts: legitimacy and support, public value created, and operational capacity. The questions to answer: Who uses the service, and who is left behind by each option? What does the public value, and how will we know we deliver it? What do elected representatives, claimants, staff, and advocates think, and why? What can the agency actually deliver and sustain? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. The people who wait longest are those least able to use a digital-only service. Test: analyze claims by route, time, and characteristics; interview claimants. Assisted digital support can bring most claimants to the digital route over time. Test: pilot in one or two offices and measure outcomes. Opposition to closures would weaken support. Test: consult local representatives and community groups early. Staff can be trained for assisted work. Test: ask staff and managers, and estimate the training time. Constraints The service must be legitimate and fair, not only efficient. Trained staff must be funded before launch. Any proposal to close an office should be a separate decision. Unknown, to be confirmed: legal duties of access and equality, the budget for the redesign, and the effect of other reforms. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Digital-only service, with some offices closed. Value: largest saving; fastest processing for those who can use it. Risks: shifts the burden to those who can least bear it; likely to meet strong opposition, weakening legitimacy. Digital-first service, with assisted routes kept. Digital is the default, local offices remain as assisted-digital centers, and a telephone route stays. Value: most of the processing benefit while protecting access. Cost drivers: staff training; running multiple channels; smaller saving. Keep the current mix and improve it. Process improvements only. Value: lowest risk; no access concerns. Risks: leaves long waits largely unchanged and does not use digital opportunities. Co-design with claimants before choosing a model, and test several service patterns in pilots. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Efficiency versus equity. How much saving is worth how much less access? Who decides? Whose voice counts? Claimants, staff, representatives, and advocates may disagree. Measures. Median processing time alone can hide unfairness. The gap between the slowest-served and fastest-served groups matters. Sustainability. Can the agency maintain assisted services over time? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Use cost-benefit thinking that includes social costs and benefits, for example as set out in public-sector appraisal guidance such as the UK Treasury's Green Book. Count benefits to claimants (time, stress, access) as well as costs to the agency. Estimate operating costs and savings of each option as ranges, including the cost of handling failed or repeat claims. Add equity and access measures: the gap in processing time between groups, success at first attempt, and use by route. Weigh options against the three parts of the strategic triangle, and consider reputational and political effects. Pilot and publish results, with named measures and decision points. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides, and what the departmental board needs to see. Agree criteria, including equity measures, and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment publicly where appropriate, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides on a digital-first service with assisted routes, it would need to: Publish the measures and report on them regularly, including gaps between groups. Fund and train staff for assisted routes before launch. Co-design the assisted service with claimants who wait longest, and publish what was learned. Treat any proposal to close an office as a new decision based on the first year's data. Related decisions Hybrid remote-work policy: staff arrangements in offices that stay open. Decisions not yet made: the office network; staffing and training plans. Related notes Open items: analyze claim data by group and route; plan consultation with representatives; set up a pilot. records.title: Reduce single-vendor concentration risk
records.text: Reduce single-vendor concentration risk Status: request for comments Date: 2026-05-20 Decision-maker(s): COO (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Procurement Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering how to respond to a heavy dependence on one vendor for critical services. It shows how a team can frame the risk, debate the options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue An internal risk review found that a large share of critical infrastructure spend goes to a single vendor. That vendor had an unplanned outage that disrupted a customer-facing service, and its prices have risen with no contractual cap. Continuing as is leaves the organization exposed to availability risk and to unchecked cost growth. The questions to answer: How much of what we depend on is actually concentrated, and what happens to the business if the vendor fails or raises prices again? How likely and how severe are those events, and what are we willing to accept? What are the realistic ways to reduce the risk, at what cost, and how fast? What would a safe exit or fallback look like? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. The outage and price rise reflect a lasting pattern , not a one-off. Test: review incident history, vendor communications, and market prices. A second vendor can run part of the critical workload at acceptable quality. Test: shortlist candidates and run a limited trial. The primary vendor will improve terms if it sees credible alternatives. Test: ask for a renewal proposal while evaluating other options. A phased migration can avoid service disruption. Test: review the technical dependencies and the contract's limits on moving workload. Constraints Customer-facing service must not be disrupted during any transition. Contract terms may limit how quickly workload can be moved, and may include charges to leave. Any new vendor should be assessed using the same criteria as the original. Unknown, to be confirmed: data portability, proprietary services in use, exit fees, and regulatory expectations about third-party risk. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Accept the risk and monitor. Value: no near-term cost or effort. Risks: leaves both outage and price exposure; the risk review may not allow it at current concentration. Renegotiate with the existing vendor for service levels, a price cap, and better exit terms; stay single-vendor. Value: addresses price and accountability. Risks: does not remove the single point of failure. Diversify: move part of the critical workload to a second vendor and renegotiate the primary contract for the rest. Value: reduces concentration; strengthens negotiating position. Cost drivers: vendor selection; migration effort; duplicate running costs for a time; added operational complexity (two sets of procedures and skills). Timeline shape: phased, with checkpoints. Build resilience without a second vendor : backups, tested recovery procedures, and design changes that make switching possible later. Move fully to another vendor. Highest disruption; justified only if the current vendor is unacceptable. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Risk appetite. What level of dependence is acceptable? Who decides? Cost of resilience. Redundancy has an ongoing price; is insurance worth it, and for which services? Complexity. Two vendors add operational complexity. Does the team have the skills? Lock-in. How much does the organization rely on one vendor's proprietary features, and what would moving cost? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Identify critical services and their dependencies. For each, estimate the business impact of an outage of different lengths, as ranges. Estimate the likelihood of failure and price change using history and vendor evidence, with uncertainty. Cost each option: migration, duplicate running costs, tooling, training, procurement, and the ongoing complexity; include exit costs for both vendors. Compare expected reduction in risk against cost, and test sensitivity to the likelihood estimates. Define leading indicators and trigger points, for example a service-level breach, a price change, or a security event. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides, and the risk appetite that applies. Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides to diversify, it would need to: Run a vendor selection process using the same criteria as the original. Plan a phased migration that avoids disruption. Renegotiate the primary contract in parallel. Accept added operational complexity, with a runbook for each vendor. Report concentration and service-level terms regularly until the target is reached. Decisions not yet made: exit and continuity plan; vendor selection. Related notes Open items: list the critical services and their vendors; collect incident history; read the contract for exit and price terms. records.title: Select a CRM platform
records.text: Select a CRM platform Status: request for comments Date: 2026-02-02 Decision-maker(s): VP Sales (to be confirmed) Owner: Sales Operations Manager Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering whether to replace its customer relationship management (CRM) system and how to choose a new one. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate the options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue The current CRM was implemented several years ago and no longer supports the automation the sales process needs: representatives spend noticeable time on manual data entry that other tools automate. The contract renews soon, which creates a natural decision point. Sales Operations, Marketing, and Finance all depend on the system and need to agree on what happens next. The questions to answer: What exactly is not working, and is it the tool, the data model, the process, or how people use it? What must a replacement do (requirements), and what would be nice to have? How do we compare vendors fairly, and what is the full cost of each choice? How do we migrate, train, and measure success? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Manual data entry is a large and avoidable burden. Test: time a sample of representatives for a few days. A modern platform would remove most of that burden. Test: ask vendors to show the work with our own data, not a standard demo. Representatives will adopt a new platform if it is well supported. Test: involve a few representatives in evaluation and ask what would make them switch or resist. Marketing and Finance integrations are achievable. Test: ask each vendor and each reference customer how that integration works in practice. Constraints The contract renews on a known date, and notice of termination must be given in time. Sales Operations, Marketing, and Finance must all agree. Customer data must stay protected during migration and afterwards; check obligations under data protection law and the vendor's security assurances. Unknown, to be confirmed: data volumes and quality, number of integrations, what can be retired, and what the vendor charges for exit. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Renew the current CRM and invest in custom automation. Value: avoids migration and retraining. Cost drivers: custom development and its maintenance; continued limits of the data model. Risks: may treat the symptom and not the cause if the vendor has no plan to improve the underlying model. Switch to a candidate platform (A). Candidate strengths and gaps to be established through requirements, demonstrations, and reference calls. Switch to another candidate platform (B). As above; compare especially support quality during migration and integration with the finance system. Choose a lighter or more focused tool if the team's real needs are narrower than a full CRM. Extend a platform the company already owns (for example a marketing or finance platform that has CRM features) to avoid adding a system. How to compare: write requirements first; ask vendors for a request for information, and a request for proposal for finalists; run scripted demonstrations using your own scenarios; speak to reference customers of similar size and complexity, including ones that have left the vendor. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Fix or replace. What would we need to believe for the current system to be good enough with better configuration or training? Price versus support. Lower price may mean weaker migration support or missing integrations that cost more later. Breadth versus fit. A broad platform may do more than needed; a focused one may be outgrown. Timing. The renewal date forces a decision, but rushing a migration can cost more than another term of the current system. How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Estimate total cost of ownership over a stated horizon in the organization's own terms: licences; implementation and data migration; integrations; training; administration; support; exit costs; and the productivity dip during change. Estimate benefit as a range: time saved per representative, better data for forecasting, fewer errors, and effects on conversion. State how each will be measured. Score vendors on a weighted matrix of requirements, usability, integration, security, support, vendor stability, and cost; ask each stakeholder group to weight criteria before seeing scores. Test sensitivity: which result would change if migration takes longer, adoption is slower, or benefits are smaller? Run a pre-mortem on the chosen option. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who must agree. Agree requirements and weights before reviewing vendors. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides to switch, it would need to: Plan a migration with a parallel-run period and validated integrations in a test environment. Train all users before cutover. Give notice to the current vendor before the term auto-renews. Accept a short-term productivity dip, and agree how to know when it has ended. Document the final migration runbook. Related decisions Contact relationship management: the wider question of how contacts and consent are handled. Enter the mid-market segment: a new sales motion may change CRM needs. Decisions not yet made: integration approach; data retention rules. Related notes Open items: list requirements from sales, marketing, and finance; collect reference customers; find out exit terms of the current vendor. records.title: Six Sigma
records.text: Six Sigma Status: request for comments Date: 2026-01-19 Decision-maker(s): Chief Operating Officer (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Quality Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering how to introduce Six Sigma, the data-driven method for reducing variation and defects, into an operation. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate the options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue An operations team handles a large volume of cases, and a meaningful share need to be redone because of errors, for example in data entry and routing. Rework costs money and time and is a leading cause of customer complaints. Leaders are interested in Six Sigma as a structured way to reduce defects, but they know that training many people at once would take staff off the line, and that the organization's data may not yet be good enough to measure defects consistently in every process. The questions to answer: What is the actual size and cost of the rework problem, and how reliably can we measure it today? Is Six Sigma the right tool for this problem, or are simpler fixes enough? Where should we start, with how many trained practitioners, and what is the first project? How do we decide whether it is working and whether to extend it? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. A small number of causes drive most of the rework. Test: sample rework cases and classify causes; look at whether a few categories dominate. We can measure defects consistently. Test: have two people count defects in the same sample and see whether they agree; check whether the data needed exists. Trained staff can run a project alongside their normal work. Test: estimate the time a DMAIC project needs against what staff can spare. Improvements will hold once the project ends. Test: ask what controls (monitoring, ownership, standard work) will keep the gain in place. The process chosen first is representative enough to teach lessons for the next one. Test: compare the first candidate with others on volume, variability, and data quality. Constraints Training everyone at once would take many people off the line. Data quality may limit what can be measured in the first stage. Customer-facing quality commitments continue while the work is under way. Unknown, to be confirmed: how project savings will be validated by finance, and what training and certification route the organization prefers. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Roll out company-wide, with belt training for managers everywhere. Value: a shared method quickly. Cost drivers: training time for many managers; projects started before they can be measured; management attention. Timeline shape: broad early effort, uneven results. Risks: removes many managers from operations; projects without reliable baselines. Adopt with a small group of trained practitioners and a single process first. Train a small group (for example Green Belts and Black Belts), choose one high-volume process, measure the defect rate, run a project using DMAIC (define, measure, analyze, improve, control), and use the result to choose the next. Value: proves value with data; builds capability where it is needed. Cost drivers: training; project time; measurement systems; sponsor time. Timeline shape: a first project from definition to sustained control, then extension only when the target has held for a stated period. Capabilities needed: statistical skills; sponsor support; reliable data. Risks: slow; benefits narrow at first. Use outside consultants to run projects. Value: speed and experience. Cost drivers: fees; the knowledge that leaves with them. Risks: little internal capability remains. Use simpler problem-solving first (for example process mapping, root-cause analysis, and error-proofing) and add Six Sigma only if needed. Cheaper, and a good baseline to cost honestly. Combine with lean methods (known together as Lean Six Sigma) if the problem is also about flow and waiting, not only variation. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Is the problem variation, or something else? Six Sigma is strongest where a process produces results that vary and defects can be counted. Is that the case here? Measurement first. Without a trustworthy way to count defects, the method cannot work. Is investing in measurement the real first project? Depth versus breadth. A few deep projects, or a broad but shallow programme? Savings claims. How will savings be validated, and by whom, so that numbers are believed? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Estimate the cost of poor quality in the organization's own terms: rework time, delays, complaints handled, lost customers. Give ranges. Estimate programme costs: training, practitioner time, measurement set-up, sponsor time, tools. Give ranges. Compare options on expected benefit, certainty of benefit, time to first result, and reversibility. Use a weighted decision matrix for value, cost, speed, risk, and capability left behind. Run a pre-mortem on the first project and add controls to prevent each reason for failure. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and by when. Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence listed above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team chooses a single-process start, it would need to: Name a sponsor, select the practitioners, and protect their time. Agree the baseline and target before the project begins, and measure them the same way before and after. Invest in measurement first if the data is not reliable. Define what "held" means (for example the target is met for a stated number of consecutive periods) before extending to other processes. Make sure managers outside the first project know when their process will be considered. Related decisions Lean manufacturing: a related approach to reducing waste. Choose our information technology frameworks: how Six Sigma fits with other frameworks. Business frameworks: the same staged-adoption pattern for another framework. Decisions not yet made: how savings are validated; training route. Related notes Open items: pick candidate processes and compare them; check data availability; list who could be a sponsor. records.title: Choose the primary database
records.text: Choose the primary database Status: request for comments Date: 2026-03-22 Decision-maker(s): CTO (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Platform Engineering Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is choosing the primary database for a growing product. It is the one technology example in this set, and shows that architecture decisions follow the same pattern as the business decisions elsewhere in this collection. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue The current database is approaching its scaling limits, and the engineering team expects growth to reach those limits before long. A replacement or a different way of scaling must be chosen before the next major product launch. The questions to answer: What are the real limits today (reads, writes, storage, latency, operations), and how fast are we approaching them? Which qualities matter most (consistency, availability, latency, cost, operability, compliance), and in what order? Do we scale what we have, move to a managed service, or run something ourselves? How would we migrate, and how would we leave again if we had to? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. The growth projection is realistic. Test: compare with past growth and with sales and product plans; consider a high and a low case. The current database can be scaled further, at a price. Test: ask the vendor and the team how much headroom remains and what it costs. Our workload fits a horizontally scalable design. Test: study queries and transactions; look for operations that need strong consistency across records. The team can operate the chosen option. Test: list the skills required and who has them. Constraints The change must be ready before the launch, with a phased migration that does not disturb it. Recurring cost must fit the approved budget. Data protection and security obligations apply to any choice. Unknown, to be confirmed: data volume, retention requirements, regional requirements, integration with other systems, and vendor commitments. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Scale the current database vertically (a larger machine or plan). Value: lowest migration risk; no application changes. Risks: buys a limited amount of time; cost rises steeply. Move to a managed, horizontally scalable database service. Value: removes scaling and much operational work; vendor support. Cost drivers: recurring service charges; migration; application changes; egress and exit costs. Risks: dependence on the vendor's features and pricing. Move to a self-hosted, horizontally scalable database. Value: potentially lower recurring cost; more control. Cost drivers: building operational skills; on-call load; tooling; upgrades. Risks: operational overhead may be higher than expected. Redesign the data layer (for example caching, read replicas, partitioning, or separating workloads) to extend the current database. Use different databases for different workloads (polyglot persistence), at the cost of more systems to run. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Consistency versus availability. The CAP theorem says a distributed system that is partitioned cannot guarantee both. Which matters more for each part of the product? Many workloads can tolerate delayed consistency; some cannot. Managed versus self-hosted. Higher service cost against lower operational risk. How should the team value the engineers' time? Lock-in. What is lost by using a vendor-specific feature, and what is gained? Standards. How much do we rely on SQL (standardized in ISO/IEC 9075) versus a vendor-specific query model? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Test with your own workload: create a realistic benchmark and measure each candidate under expected and peak load, including failure scenarios. Estimate total cost of ownership over a stated horizon in the organization's own terms: service or licence charges, hosting, migration, engineering time, on-call, training, support, and exit. Show ranges. Score candidates on a weighted matrix of the qualities that matter (the ISO/IEC 25010 product quality model offers a vocabulary for this), and test sensitivity to the weights. Estimate how long each option buys, and what it costs when the limit is reached again. Plan for exit: how would data and code move away from each choice? Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who must be consulted (security, finance, product). Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above, including benchmark results, and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides to migrate, it would need to: Plan a phased migration with a parallel-run period before full cutover. Confirm budget for the recurring costs. Plan follow-on decisions, for example on connection pooling and read replicas. Record the expected exit path. Related decisions Build vs. buy for a project: general build/buy reasoning. Reduce single-vendor concentration risk: dependence on one vendor. Decisions not yet made: caching and replica strategy; data retention. Related notes Open items: collect production metrics; write down workload characteristics; shortlist candidates for a benchmark. records.title: Enter the mid-market segment
records.text: Enter the mid-market segment Status: request for comments Date: 2026-03-10 Decision-maker(s): CEO, with Board input (to be confirmed) Owner: VP Strategy Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering whether and how to extend a go-to-market approach built for large customers to a mid-sized customer segment. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate the options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue A company that sells to large enterprise customers sees its pipeline flattening and its win rate staying flat, while inbound interest from smaller companies is growing. Today it either turns this demand away or serves it poorly with a sales approach designed for large deals. The board wants a credible growth path beyond saturation of the enterprise segment. The questions the team must answer: Is the mid-market segment attractive for us (size, growth, needs we can meet, competition)? Can we win and serve it profitably with our product, price, and sales approach, or does something need to change? How should we enter, and with what resources, given that new hiring may not be possible? What would tell us early that it is working or not? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Mid-market buyers decide faster but spend less per customer. Test: interview recent mid-sized prospects and look at deal length and size in the data we already have. The product needs modest simplification to suit mid-market onboarding. Test: watch mid-sized customers use it, and list the steps that cause confusion. Existing sales talent can adapt to a faster, lighter-touch approach. Test: ask the sales team what they would need, and look at who has done this before. Entering the segment will not harm enterprise results. Test: estimate how much enterprise capacity the move would take, and from which teams. Constraints No new hiring may be approved this year; any move must be funded from existing budget. Enterprise revenue commitments for the current year must not be put at risk. Contract terms built for large buyers may be too heavy for faster deals; Legal has flagged this. Unknown, to be confirmed: the size of the segment in our territories, pricing the segment will accept, and support load. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Stay enterprise-only and invest further in enterprise expansion. Value: lowest execution risk; builds on what works. Risks: does not address the flat pipeline; skeptics doubt it reaches growth targets alone. Enter with a dedicated new team. Value: cleanest execution and focus. Cost drivers: recruiting, onboarding, salaries, management time; blocked if hiring is frozen. Timeline shape: slow to start because of hiring; long ramp. Enter by reallocating part of existing enterprise sales capacity , with a simplified onboarding process. Value: fundable now; reversible if it underperforms; real data on mid-market economics before a larger commitment. Cost drivers: lost enterprise coverage; retraining; product and legal work for simpler onboarding and terms. Capabilities needed: a pod with clear leadership; product changes; simplified contract terms. Risks: slower ramp than a dedicated team; enterprise pipeline suffers. Enter through channel or reseller partners. Value: lowest internal cost; reach. Cost drivers: partner margin, enablement, partner management. Risks: weaker control of the customer relationship; results may lag direct sales (check with peer companies). Serve the segment with a self-serve product and no sales involvement. Test willingness to buy without contact. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Growth versus focus. Does adding a segment dilute what makes the company good at enterprise? Speed versus reversibility. Which options can be undone cheaply if the assumptions prove wrong? Who pays for it? Reallocation protects the budget but moves cost into lost enterprise attention. Position. Using the Ansoff matrix, selling an existing product to a new market (market development) is less risky than also changing the product (diversification). Where does this move sit? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Size the opportunity as a range: number of target firms, share reachable, expected deal value, win rate, and sales cycle, with clearly labelled assumptions. Cost the entry: capacity moved, product changes, legal work, marketing, partner terms, and the opportunity cost of what enterprise sales would otherwise do. Compare options under best, likely, and worst scenarios; compare payback period and learning value. Choose leading indicators in advance: qualified opportunities, conversion at each stage, time to close, and cost to acquire a customer, along with effects on enterprise pipeline. Use a weighted matrix (value, cost, speed, reversibility, risk to the core business) and a pre-mortem. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides, and what the board needs to see. Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team chooses a staged entry, it would need to: Name which capacity moves, and when, and what happens to enterprise targets. Plan product, legal, and onboarding work that the segment needs. Agree checkpoints (for example at the end of two periods) with clear criteria for continuing, expanding, or stopping. Report segment results to the board in a consistent way. Related decisions Usage-based pricing: pricing for a new segment may need rethinking. Select a CRM platform: the tools sales uses may need to change for a faster sales motion. Decisions not yet made: pricing and packaging for the segment; partner strategy; next year's staffing. Related notes Open items: interview recent mid-sized prospects; list reasons for lost and won deals; ask Legal for a lighter set of terms. records.title: Target operating model
records.text: Target operating model Status: request for comments Date: 2026-09-15 Decision-maker(s): CEO and executive team (to be confirmed) Owner: Chief Operating Officer Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering how to describe and move toward a target operating model: how the organization will deliver its strategy through processes, people, technology, locations, and governance. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue An organization has grown by acquisition and by hiring, and its structure now reflects that history rather than a plan. Business units run their own finance, support, and procurement; customers meet different teams, systems, and prices depending on which unit they first contacted; leaders cannot say who is accountable for end-to-end outcomes such as onboarding a customer. The questions to answer: What must the organization be able to do to deliver its strategy, and where does the current structure prevent it? What are the realistic ways to organize, and what does each give up? Which parts should be shared and which should stay close to customers? How would the organization move there in stages, and how would people be treated during the change? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Duplicated functions are a real cost, not just an irritation. Test: map one function across units and compare the effort and results. Customers notice the inconsistency. Test: trace customer journeys across units; look at complaints and effort. Shared services can meet the needs of teams that depend on them. Test: ask the dependent teams what service levels they would need. Delivery should stay close to customers. Test: ask leaders of large units what would be lost if delivery were centralized. Constraints The target must be described in a single document covering processes, roles, technology, locations, and governance. The change must be staged, and the order of moves is a separate decision. People affected need clear, fair treatment, and no one should learn of an individual outcome before it is decided; take advice on employment law. Unknown, to be confirmed: which systems would need to be unified, and contract and regulatory constraints. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Keep the business-unit model and harmonize at the edges. Value: lowest disruption; keeps local autonomy. Risks: leaves duplicated functions and an inconsistent customer experience. Move to a functional model in which sales, delivery, finance, and support each become company-wide functions. Value: removes duplication; clear functional standards. Risks: separates teams from the customers and products they serve; delivery speed may suffer. Hybrid: shared services plus customer-aligned teams. Finance, people, procurement, and support become shared services; sales and delivery stay aligned to customer segments. Value: much of the efficiency of the functional model while keeping delivery close to customers. Cost drivers: design effort; service-level agreements; systems; transition costs; management time. Risks: the most complex to design and run. Different models for different parts of the business , chosen deliberately. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Autonomy versus consistency. How much local freedom is worth the duplication? Where does the customer meet us? Organizing around customers and organizing around functions pull in different directions (Conway's law notes that organizations tend to produce designs that mirror their communication structures). Service levels. Shared services work only if the teams that depend on them trust the commitments. Pace. A staged approach lowers risk but prolongs the period of mixed models. How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Define design principles and desired outcomes first, such as onboarding time, cost of shared services, customer satisfaction by segment, and accountability for end-to-end results. Estimate transition costs and ongoing costs of each model in the organization's terms: change effort, systems, redundancy or reassignment, management time, and temporary loss of output. Show ranges. Test each model against realistic customer journeys and incidents. Compare options on value, cost, risk, speed, and people impact, using a weighted matrix. Agree a review point against the outcome measures set in the document. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides, and who must be consulted. Agree design principles and criteria first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides to move to a hybrid model, it would need to: Name an owner for the target operating model document and a date for its first version. Publish service levels and named owners for each shared service before any team is moved onto it. Decide separately how role changes are handled. Review the model against the outcome measures after a stated period. Related decisions Business frameworks: how to approach staged change. Project portfolio management: how projects are chosen under the target model. Choose between a product business and a service business: strategic choices that affect the model. Decisions not yet made: order and timing of moves; treatment of role changes. Related notes Open items: map the current structure; collect customer journey examples; agree design principles. records.title: Written ways of working
records.text: Written ways of working Status: request for comments Date: 2026-04-27 Decision-maker(s): Head of Engineering (to be confirmed) Owner: Engineering Manager Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering whether to write down shared ways of working (principles, ground rules, and team agreements) as a group grows. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue A product and engineering group has grown quickly, and expectations that used to be understood are now different between teams: how quickly to answer a message, when a decision needs a meeting, how to disagree, and what counts as done. New joiners report learning these by making mistakes. The group needs ways of working that are explicit, understood, open to debate, and quick to flag when someone breaks them. The questions to answer: Which expectations differ most, and which of those cause real problems? What should be common to the whole group, and what should each team decide? How should agreements be written, kept, found, and changed? How will we know whether they help? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Most friction comes from unstated expectations , not from disagreement about them. Test: ask people to describe how decisions get made and compare the answers. Teams keep agreements they wrote themselves. Test: pilot with a team and review after a while. A short shared set is enough. Test: draft a few principles and ask people if they would read and use them. People feel safe to raise problems. Test: ask; psychological safety, as studied by Amy Edmondson and others, is a condition for any agreement to work. Constraints The group-wide set must be short enough to read in a few minutes. Teams have limited time to write and review agreements. Agreements must be kept where new joiners find them on their first day. Unknown, to be confirmed: the differing needs of design, engineering, and support. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Rely on culture and onboarding conversations. Value: no effort. Risks: already failing for people who join later. Adopt one company-wide set of ways of working. Value: consistency. Risks: written by a few, may feel imposed; may not fit very different teams. Write a short group-wide set and let each team add its own working agreement. Value: consistency and ownership. Cost drivers: team time to write and review; a place to keep and find agreements; someone to maintain the shared set. Start with one or two teams , learn what works, then extend. Use a published model (for example Team Topologies for team interaction modes) as a starting vocabulary, adapted to local needs. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Rules or principles? Principles invite judgement; rules are easier to check. Who writes? A few leaders, or everyone? Participation builds ownership but takes time. How binding? What happens when someone breaks an agreement, and who raises it? Change. If anyone can propose changes, how are they decided? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Estimate the cost of the current approach: time lost to misunderstanding, slow onboarding, repeated discussions. Estimate the cost of writing and maintaining agreements: facilitation, review meetings, tools. Choose measures: onboarding feedback, number of repeated disputes, results of short pulse surveys, and whether people can say where agreements are and how to change them. Compare the options on value, cost, and speed; decide how and when to review. Try a pilot and define in advance what a good result would be. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who is consulted. Agree criteria first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides on a short shared set plus team agreements, it would need to: Name who drafts the shared set, who reviews, and when it is published. Ask each team to write its agreement soon after publication and to keep it where new joiners find it. Make each agreement name who handles a breakage. Review agreements regularly and check twice a year that people know them. Related decisions The Agile Manifesto: shared values and team practice. Decisions not yet made: tooling for keeping agreements; how conflicts between team agreements are resolved. Related notes Open items: collect examples of differing expectations; ask new joiners what surprised them; choose a pilot team. records.title: Workplace planning and management
records.text: Workplace planning and management Status: request for comments Date: 2026-10-08 Decision-maker(s): Chief Operating Officer (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Workplace Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is considering how to plan and manage its workplace as one system, using evidence of how space is used. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision. Issue After the organization chose team-set anchor days for hybrid working, office use became much harder to predict: some days are busy and others nearly empty, and teams that share a floor have found no room to meet on the same day. Space, desks, meeting rooms, cleaning, and security are managed by separate groups with separate data. The organization needs a way to plan and manage the workplace as one system, so that space fits the work and the property budget is well spent. The questions to answer: How is space really used (by day, floor, and type of space), and what do people need? What data can be collected without being intrusive or unlawful, and how will staff be told? Who owns the whole picture? How do we adjust space over time, including the lease? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Aggregated data shows how space is used without tracking individuals. Test: define the data, check that it cannot be traced to individuals, and review with privacy specialists. Teams will book their zones for the days of their agreements. Test: pilot with a few teams. Fitting desks and rooms to demand reduces waste. Test: compare occupancy with capacity over several weeks and different seasons. Staff will accept shared desks if booking works well. Test: ask, and run a pilot. Constraints Usage should be reported only in aggregate (by floor and by day), never about individuals. Staff must be told how data is used before it is collected; privacy law applies (for example the GDPR in Europe). Adjustments for individuals are handled through a separate process and must not be hindered by booking rules. Unknown, to be confirmed: lease break points, existing systems, and accessibility needs. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Keep managing space by group. Value: no change in effort. Risks: decisions continue to conflict; no overall picture. Buy an integrated workplace management platform and let it assign desks. Value: complete data and automation. Cost drivers: licences; integration; configuration; change management. Risks: automatic assignment may ignore what teams need to be together. Plan from usage data, with team bookings. One owner for space, bookings, and services; badge, booking, and sensor-free data; a regular plan of space by day; bookable team zones. Value: matches space to demand and keeps teams together. Cost drivers: data work; booking tool; the owner's time. Survey-based approach using regular staff surveys and observation instead of automated data, at lower privacy risk but less precision. Pilot on one floor before extending. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Data versus privacy. What is the minimum data needed, and what would staff accept? Choice versus coordination. Fixed desks give stability; shared desks give efficiency. Ownership. Combining groups into one function has people effects. Lease. Reducing space saves cost, but removing it is hard to undo. How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Measure occupancy and booking patterns over a meaningful period and compare with capacity. Cost the options: space (existing and scenarios), systems, booking tools, staff time, change effort, and moves. Show ranges. Consider benefits: space savings, better team co-location, lower service costs, better experience. Assess privacy risk and mitigations, with specialist input; consider ISO/IEC 27701 and privacy-by-design thinking. Review after the first year of data, using named measures. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who is consulted (including privacy and employee representatives). Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides on usage-based planning with bookable team zones, it would need to: Name an owner for space, bookings, cleaning, and security services. Publish a regular plan of space by day. Tell staff how data is collected and used before collecting it. Fit desks and rooms to measured demand, which may mean fewer fixed desks and more meeting space. Review the lease at the next break point using a year of data. Related decisions Choose a hybrid working model: the policy this supports. Workplace reasonable adjustments: individual needs. Decisions not yet made: booking tool; lease terms. Related notes Open items: gather occupancy data; draft a data and privacy statement; choose a pilot floor. records.title: Workplace reasonable adjustments
records.text: Workplace reasonable adjustments Status: request for comments Date: 2026-03-30 Decision-maker(s): Chief People Officer (to be confirmed) Owner: Head of Employee Experience Summary: Work in progress. This is a starting point for a team that is designing a clear, fast, private, and fair process for workplace adjustments for disabled employees and candidates. It shows how a team can frame the question, debate options, and gather information. It records no decision and is not legal advice. Issue In many places the law requires employers to make reasonable adjustments (called reasonable accommodations in some countries) so that a disabled employee or candidate is not at a disadvantage, and it is also simply the right way to treat people. Requests are currently handled differently by each manager: some people wait a long time, some are asked to explain their condition repeatedly, and some are refused with no reason given. Managers say they do not know what is reasonable or who pays. The questions to answer: What do the laws in the places where we operate require, and what do good practice and our values ask beyond that? What do employees and candidates experience now, and what would they want? Who decides, who pays, how fast, and how is privacy protected? How do we handle a refusal, an appeal, and a change in circumstances? Assumptions Each assumption is something to test. Inconsistent handling is a real problem. Test: review recent requests (without identifying individuals) for time taken, outcome, and reasons given. People can describe what they need without disclosing a diagnosis. Test: ask employees and advisers, and look at how guidance from bodies such as Acas or the Job Accommodation Network frames requests. Managers can decide well with training and an adviser. Test: talk with managers about what they would need. A central budget improves fairness. Test: check how costs are paid today and whether cost has influenced outcomes. Constraints Legal requirements differ by country and region; take local legal advice. This record is not legal advice. Refusals must be given in writing with the reason and a route to appeal. Managers should not be told a diagnosis unless the person chooses to share it. Unknown, to be confirmed: volume and cost of requests, the occupational health or adviser capacity, and relevant collective agreements. Options considered For each option, estimate value, costs, timeline, and capability needs, and note what evidence would change the team's mind. Leave it to line managers. Value: decisions close to the person and the job. Risks: inconsistent results; managers untrained for the decision; medical detail exposed to more people than necessary. Send every request to a central team. Value: consistency and privacy. Risks: slow for simple requests; the team may not understand the role. A central team sets the process and pays; managers decide on advice. The person describes what they need, not their diagnosis; the manager and the person agree an adjustment, using a trained adviser where needed, with a central budget. Value: fast for simple requests, consistent, and fair on cost. Cost drivers: the budget; the adviser; training; administration. Tiered process. Simple requests are agreed locally and quickly; complex ones go to an adviser. Use an external provider for assessments and advice. Argument Points of debate the team should expect: Speed versus consistency. How can simple requests be decided fast without losing fairness? Privacy. What does a manager need to know, and what must stay confidential? What is reasonable. Legal tests (for example in the UK Equality Act 2010, or the US Americans with Disabilities Act) consider factors such as effectiveness, cost, and practicability. How will the organization apply them consistently? Cost. Who pays, and how does the organization avoid cost deciding the outcome? How the team could evaluate costs and trade-offs: Estimate the volume and type of requests from past data, and the likely cost range, including one-off and recurring adjustments. Estimate the cost of the process itself: a central budget, adviser time, training, and administration. Count the costs of not acting well: time lost, attrition, legal exposure, and harm to people. Compare options on speed, consistency, privacy, fairness, cost, and legal risk, and involve disabled employees in the weighting. Choose measures such as time to agreement, satisfaction, number of refusals and appeals, and cost, reported in aggregate without identifying individuals. Decision Not yet decided. This is a starting point. A team using it should replace this section with its own decision. Suggested way to reach a decision: Confirm who decides and who is consulted, including employee representatives. Agree criteria and weights first. Gather the evidence above and record what was found. Share for comment, then decide and update the Status. Implications If the team decides on a central budget with decisions between the person and their manager, it would need to: Publish the process, form, expected timelines, and a guide for managers. Train managers before they handle requests. Set up the budget and an adviser. Review adjustments when a person's role or health changes. Report requests, timing, and cost each year without identifying individuals. Related decisions Choose a hybrid working model: working arrangements for individuals within a hybrid model. Workplace planning and management: how space and booking rules take account of individual needs. Decisions not yet made: local legal review; provider choice. Related notes Open items: review past requests; ask disabled employees what works and what does not; get local legal advice.
